one_sentence_story: In his landmark 1954 theory, Leon Festinger showed that whenever objective rulers are blurry, humans evaluate themselves against nearby peers with a relentless 'drive upward' — the exact mechanism behind why 3rd-place Bronze medalists smile wider than 2nd-place Silver medalists and why curated social feeds hijack happiness.
so_what_for_you: Use two science-backed switches whenever comparison stings: turn **upward comparison** into a concrete *'What specific skill can I learn from them?'* note, and measure your worth on **Temporal Comparison** (*'Me today vs Me last year'*).

jargon_map.plain: human drive to measure our own worth and abilities against other people whenever objective physical standards are absent
jargon_map.analogy: checking neighboring runners' pace when there are no mile markers on the road

jargon_map.plain: finding that comparison stings and motivates strongest against peers close to our own background and level, not distant superstars
jargon_map.analogy: ignoring Picasso while obsessing over your cousin's painting

jargon_map.plain: comparing yourself to someone slightly ahead ('Silver looking at Gold' — sting or inspiration) vs someone behind ('Bronze looking at 4th place' — relief & gratitude)
jargon_map.analogy: which way you turn your head on the Olympic podium

jargon_map.plain: tendency in achievement cultures for 'good enough' to perpetually shift 10% above your current peer group
jargon_map.analogy: a horizon line that moves forward every mile you walk

jargon_map.plain: measuring progress against your OWN past baseline rather than curated strangers
jargon_map.analogy: the scoreboard chronically happy people actually use
